entry: English biostatistician and mathematician. He is credited with establishing mathematical statistics as a discipline and founded the world's first university statistics department at University College London in 1911. He applied quantitative methods to biological inheritance and contributed significantly to biometrics. As a protégé and biographer of [[Francis Galton]], he edited and completed William Kingdon Clifford's *Common Sense of the Exact Sciences* (1885) and Isaac Todhunter's *History of the Theory of Elasticity* after their deaths. His innovations included the [[Chi-squared test|chi-squared test]] for goodness-of-fit and the product-moment [[Correlation|correlation coefficient]], developed in 1895. He was also a proponent of Social Darwinism and [[Eugenics|eugenics]], and his thought is today described as an example of scientific racism.

Austrian-British philosopher of science. Popper is known for rejecting the classical inductivist view of the [[Scientific method|scientific method]] in favor of empirical falsification, made possible by his falsifiability criterion. He held that a theory in the empirical sciences can never be proven, only falsified, and he replaced justificationist accounts of [[Epistemology|knowledge]] with critical rationalism. After fleeing Nazi persecution in 1937, he settled in New Zealand and later founded the Department of Philosophy at the [[London School of Economics|London School of Economics and Political Science]]. His *The Logic of Scientific Discovery* appeared in German in 1934 and in English in 1959. In political thought he defended liberal democracy and piecemeal social engineering as the basis of an open society. In *The Open Society and Its Enemies* (1945) he criticized historicism and [[Totalitarianism|totalitarianism]], and targeted [[Karl Marx|Marx]], Plato and Hegel; the interpretation of that critique remains debated.

German mathematician regarded as the father of modern analysis. He left university without a degree but studied mathematics privately, trained as a schoolteacher, and taught mathematics, [[Physics|physics]], [[Botany|botany]] and [[Gymnastics|gymnastics]]. After receiving an honorary doctorate from the University of Königsberg in 1854, he took a chair at the Gewerbeinstitut in Berlin in 1856 and became a professor at the University of Berlin in 1864. He formalized the definition of [[Continuous function|continuity]] of a function and of [[Complex analysis|complex analysis]]. He proved the intermediate value theorem and the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem, and in 1872 constructed the first continuous but nowhere differentiable function. His students included [[Georg Cantor]], Felix Klein and Hermann Minkowski. He tutored Sofia Kovalevskaya, whom he regarded as his best student, and helped her obtain a doctorate from Heidelberg University.

German composer and a leading figure of the Darmstadt School. He is known for pioneering [[Electronic music|electronic music]], for introducing controlled chance into serial composition, and for musical spatialization. Educated in [[Cologne]], he produced early breakthrough works such as *Gesang der Jünglinge* (1955–1956), which blended electronically manipulated boy soprano vocals with synthesized tones. His output of more than 300 compositions, written over nearly sixty years, ranges from pieces for musical boxes to a seven-opera cycle, *Licht*. His works influenced jazz and popular music as well as art music, and his theoretical writings comprise ten large volumes. His later adoption of esoteric philosophies, including claims of extraterrestrial origins, drew controversy.

Ancient Indian concept of action and its consequences. In Indian religions, karma denotes a principle of cause and effect in which intent and actions shape an individual's future. Good intent and good deeds produce good karma and happier rebirths, while bad intent and bad deeds produce worse rebirths. In [[Hinduism]], karma is traditionally classified into four types: *sanchita* (accumulated karma from past lifetimes), *prārabdha* (the portion now bearing fruit), *āgāmi* (future karma generated by present actions) and *kriyamāṇa* (karma created by current actions, which may yield results now or later). The concept is closely associated with rebirth in [[Buddhism]], [[Jainism]], [[Sikhism]] and [[Taoism]]. Jain thought treats karma as subtle material particles that bind the soul. Scholars debate whether karma is a theory, a model or a metaphor.

State on the southwestern coast of India (pop., 2011: 61,130,704). Formed as Mysore State in 1956 and renamed in 1973, it is the eighth-largest Indian state by population and the sixth-largest by area, at 191,791 sq km. Its capital, [[Bengaluru]], is known as the Silicon Valley of India for its information technology sector. [[Kannada]] is the principal official language. The state includes the [[Western Ghats]] and the [[Deccan Plateau]], and it was the heartland of dynasties including the [[Vijayanagara Empire]]. Karnataka has contributed significantly to both Carnatic and Hindustani classical music.

Colombian singer-songwriter. Raised in [[Medellín]], Karol G is considered one of the most influential reggaeton and urban pop artists. She received her first [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] in 2024 and has won ten Latin Grammy Awards. Her 2023 album *Mañana Será Bonito* was the first Spanish-language album by a female artist to debut at number one on the US Billboard 200. Her 2019 single "China" became her first music video with over one billion views on [[YouTube]]. In 2025 she was announced as the first Latina headliner of the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival in 2026.

Topography formed by the dissolution of soluble carbonate rocks such as [[Limestone|limestone]] and dolomite. Its features include [[Sinkhole|sinkholes]], [[Cave|caves]] and underground drainage systems, which may leave few rivers or lakes on the surface. Karst is most strongly developed in thinly bedded, highly fractured limestone and is poorly developed in chalk, which is porous rather than dense. The term derives from a limestone plateau on the border between [[Italy]] and [[Slovenia]]. Karst [[Aquifer|aquifers]] are highly permeable, which makes them vulnerable to pollutants entering the water supply. Buried karst is important in petroleum geology, because as much as 50% of the world's hydrocarbon reserves are hosted in carbonate rock.

Hindu god of war. Also known as Skanda, Subrahmanya, Shanmukha or Muruga, he is generally described as the son of [[Shiva]] and [[Parvati]] and the brother of [[Ganesha]]. He has been important in the [[Indian subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]] since ancient times. He is typically shown riding a peacock and carrying a spear called the vel, and some icons show him with six heads. In South India, where he is worshipped as Muruga, he is regarded as the patron deity of the [[Tamil language]]. He is also worshipped in Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and the Caribbean.

Language family indigenous to the South Caucasus, spoken primarily in [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]]. It comprises four closely related languages: [[Georgian language|Georgian]], Svan, Mingrelian and Laz. The family is not related to any other language family in the world. Georgian, with about 4 million speakers, is the most widely spoken member and the only literary language in the family. Svan has approximately 35,000–40,000 native speakers, while Laz is endangered as its speakers shift to Turkish. Georgian scripts are used to write all Kartvelian languages. The earliest known written record of any Kartvelian language is an Old Georgian inscription near [[Bethlehem]], dated to c. 430 AD.

Northernmost geographical region of the [[Indian subcontinent]]. Until the mid-19th century the name referred only to the Kashmir Valley; it now also covers territory administered by India, Pakistan and China, including Ladakh, Azad Kashmir, Gilgit-Baltistan and Aksai Chin. The region was an important center of [[Buddhism]] in the first millennium, and Shah Mir became its first Muslim ruler in 1339. Mughal rule began with [[Akbar]]'s conquest of Kashmir in 1586. In 1846 Gulab Singh, Raja of Jammu, became ruler of Jammu and Kashmir, and his descendants governed it under British paramountcy until the [[Partition of India]] in 1947, after which the region became disputed. Neutral sources use the terms Pakistan-administered Kashmir and India-administered Kashmir. In 2019 India revoked the special autonomy of Jammu and Kashmir, a step that Pakistani and separatist perspectives have accused of demographic engineering and suppression.

Jewish dietary laws governing which foods are permitted and how they must be prepared. Kosher foods come from permitted mammals, birds and [[Fish|fish]] that meet specific criteria; forbidden animals include [[Pork|pork]], [[Frog|frogs]] and shellfish. Because blood may not be eaten, mammals and birds must be slaughtered by a certified ritual slaughterer (*shochet*) in a process called shechita, and the meat must then be koshered by broiling, roasting, or soaking and salting. Meat and dairy may never be mixed, and separate equipment is used for meat-based and dairy-based foods. Kosher products are classified as meat (fleishig), dairy (milchig) or pareve (neutral). Most basic laws derive from Leviticus and Deuteronomy in the [[Torah]], and details are set down in the Oral Torah, codified in the [[Talmud]].

Downslope wind caused by a flow of dense, cool [[Air mass|air]] into lighter air below. Katabatic winds are usually cool or cold, because cold air is denser than warm air. The most common type forms at night as slopes cool by radiation. Examples include the piteraq of [[Greenland]], the Bora in the Adriatic and the Santa Ana winds of [[Southern California]]. Off the ice sheets of [[Antarctica]] and Greenland, they can blow well over hurricane force in coastal valleys. In parts of continental Antarctica they scour away snow, creating dry valleys such as the McMurdo Dry Valleys.

One of two Japanese syllabaries, used mainly for foreign loanwords. The name means *fragmentary kana*, because its characters derive from fragments of more complex [[Kanji|kanji]]. It evolved from Japanese Buddhist monks' transliterations of Chinese texts. Katakana transcribes foreign words (*gairaigo*) and foreign names, and is used for onomatopoeia, emphasis, technical and scientific terms, and the names of plants, animals, minerals and many Japanese companies. It contrasts with [[Hiragana|hiragana]], which writes native words and grammatical inflections. Its usage is comparable to italics in English.

Japanese sword with a curved, single-edged blade and a long grip for two hands. Developed later than the tachi, it was worn by [[Samurai|samurai]] in feudal Japan with the edge facing upward. The name is a compound of *kata* ("one side") and *na* ("blade") and first appears in the *Nihon Shoki* of 720. Its blade is generally longer than 2 shaku, or about 60 cm. In the relatively peaceful [[Edo period]], it grew in importance, and at the end of that period *shishi* political activists used it as their main weapon. In the [[Sengoku period]] of the 16th century, the main battlefield weapons were the bow, the spear and the gun, while the katana was used mainly for close combat. The Portuguese adopted the word *catana* for a [[Machete|machete]].

English singer-songwriter, musician and record producer. Noted for her eclectic style, unconventional lyrics and innovative dance performances, she became the first female artist to top the UK singles chart with a fully self-written song, "[[Wuthering Heights]]" (1978). Her albums *Never for Ever* (1980) and *Hounds of Love* (1985) both reached number one in the UK. She has produced all her studio albums since *The Dreaming* (1982). In 2022, "Running Up That Hill" (1985) reached number one in the UK after its use in the Netflix series *Stranger Things*.

English model and entrepreneur. Moss rose to fame in the early 1990s as part of the heroin chic trend, and her [[Calvin Klein]] campaigns with [[Mark Wahlberg]] made her a fashion icon. She became a contributing fashion editor for [[Vogue (magazine)|British Vogue]] and has had her own clothing range and fragrances. [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named her one of the world's 100 most influential people in 2007. A drug-use scandal in September 2005 led to her being dropped from fashion campaigns; she was cleared of charges and resumed modeling.

American fashion designer and entrepreneur. Spade co-founded the handbag brand Kate Spade New York in 1993 with Andy Spade, Elyce Arons and Pamela Bell. Its handbags, priced at US$150 to $450, became popular in [[New York City|New York]]. Before launching the label she was a senior fashion editor at *Mademoiselle*, where she had noticed a lack of stylish, affordable handbags. In 2006 Liz Claiborne bought the company for $125 million, and Coach acquired it in 2017 for $2.4 billion.

English actress known for headstrong characters in independent films and period dramas. She won a BAFTA Award for *Sense and Sensibility* (1995) and gained global stardom in *Titanic* (1997), then the highest-grossing film of its time. For playing a former Nazi camp guard in *The Reader* (2008), she won the Academy Award for Best Actress. She also received two Primetime Emmy Awards, for *Mildred Pierce* (2011) and *Mare of Easttown* (2021). A co-founder of the Golden Hat Foundation, which aims to create [[Autism|autism]] awareness, she has also written a book on the topic.

American stage and screen actress known for strong-willed, independent characters. Her six-decade career included comedies, literary dramas and Shakespearean stage roles, and she won a record four [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for Best Actress: for *Morning Glory* (1933), *Guess Who's Coming to Dinner* (1967), *The Lion in Winter* (1968) and *On Golden Pond* (1981). After the commercial failure of *Bringing Up Baby* (1938), she bought out her contract with RKO and starred in *The Philadelphia Story* (1940). Under contract to [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] in the 1940s, she made nine films with [[Spencer Tracy]]. Hepburn shunned the Hollywood publicity machine and later focused on television films.

Eleventh-century [[Sanskrit]] collection of Indian legends and folk tales, compiled by Somadeva, a Shaiva [[Brahmin|Brahman]] of Kashmir. It was written between 1063 and 1081 for the amusement of Queen Sūryavatī, wife of King Ananta of Kashmir. The work is framed by the adventures of Prince Naravahanadatta, son of King Udayana, and as many as 350 tales are built around this central story, making it the largest existing collection of Indian tales. Somadeva described it as an abridged translation of the lost *Bṛhatkathā* by Guṇāḍhya. Its tales, like those of the *Panchatantra*, traveled widely, and a Persian version was commissioned by [[Akbar]] in 1589.

American mathematician whose [[Orbital mechanics|orbital mechanics]] calculations at [[NASA]] and its predecessor, the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, were critical to the first and subsequent U.S. crewed spaceflights. She calculated trajectories and launch windows for Project Mercury, including for [[Astronaut|astronauts]] Alan Shepard and John Glenn, and rendezvous paths for the [[Apollo program|Apollo]] flights to the Moon. In 2015 [[Barack Obama|President Barack Obama]] awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. She was portrayed by Taraji P. Henson in the film *Hidden Figures* (2016).

American actress known for her deep, husky voice. She rose to prominence as Matty Walker in *Body Heat* (1981), which brought her a reputation as a [[Sex symbol|sex symbol]]. She was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Peggy Sue Got Married* (1986). Her voice work includes Jessica Rabbit in *Who Framed Roger Rabbit* (1988), and she has voiced characters on television series including *The Simpsons* and *Rick and Morty*. Turner has received two Golden Globes.

Capital and largest city of [[Nepal]] (pop., 2021: 845,767), in the central Kathmandu Valley. It is the country's main governmental, financial, industrial and cultural center, at an elevation of 1,324 m (4,344 ft). The surrounding metropolitan area has about 4 million people. Known as Kantipur in medieval times, the city takes its name from Kasthamandap, a three-story pavilion made entirely of wood and rebuilt in 1596. It served as the royal capital of the Kingdom of Nepal, and several of its heritage sites are [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Sites]], including Durbar Square and Pashupatinath. Since 1985 it has hosted the headquarters of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).

American actress. Baker began her career in theater, and her screen debut was in *The Right Stuff* (1983). She received the National Society of Film Critics Award for Best Supporting Actress for *Street Smart* (1987). She has appeared in over 50 films, including *Edward Scissorhands* (1990) and *Cold Mountain* (2003). On television she starred as Dr. Jill Brock in the [[CBS]] drama *Picket Fences* (1992–1996), for which she won three Primetime Emmy Awards.
